option_identity: $3.20 million
option_text: $3.20 million
why_wrong: This is BAC/CPI = 2.40/0.75 = 3.20 (CPI=EV/AC=0.90/1.20=0.75), which assumes the historical cost inefficiency continues for all remaining work -- but the stem explicitly states the overrun was a one-time, already-corrected procurement issue and remaining work is expected at the ORIGINAL budgeted rate, contradicting that assumption.
governing_concept: An EAC method (or a decision to keep using BAC as the forecast) is only valid when the continuing-performance assumption it embeds actually matches the performance data and scenario given.
corrective_rule: EAC = AC + (BAC-EV) when the stem states remaining work continues at the ORIGINAL budgeted rate (as it explicitly does here, since the overrun was a one-time, already-corrected issue) -- not BAC/CPI (which assumes the historical, now-resolved inefficiency continues) and not BAC unchanged (which assumes zero variance at all).
exam_trap: Stale-assumption trap: an EAC method (or BAC-as-forecast) whose embedded continuing-performance assumption contradicts the CPI/trend data actually stated.
calculation_path_if_applicable: BAC/CPI = 2.40/0.75 = $3.20 million (wrong assumption: historical inefficiency continues).

option_identity: Approve the transfer because any unfavorable control-account variance is automatically an unknown-unknown
option_text: Approve the transfer because any unfavorable control-account variance is automatically an unknown-unknown
why_wrong: This mischaracterizes an already-occurred, already-accumulated cost overrun (a known, realized event) as an 'unknown-unknown' (the risk category MR is meant to cover), which is precisely the prohibited use of MR: offsetting a known, accumulated over-run rather than an unforeseen future risk event.
governing_concept: Management Reserve sits outside the Performance Measurement Baseline, has no assigned scope, and prudent-use rules explicitly prohibit using it to offset accumulated cost or schedule over/under-runs that have already occurred in existing control accounts.
corrective_rule: MR may never be used to erase or absorb an already-accumulated, already-occurred control-account variance.
exam_trap: Overrun-absorption trap: Management Reserve is proposed to offset an already-accumulated control-account overrun, contrary to prudent-use rules.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_identity: Move the overrun to undistributed budget so the original control-account performance is preserved
option_text: Move the overrun to undistributed budget so the original control-account performance is preserved
why_wrong: Relocating the overrun into undistributed budget to preserve the control account's reported performance masks a real, already-occurred cost problem through budget reclassification rather than addressing it -- historical performance should remain visible, not be hidden by moving costs between PMB components.
governing_concept: The Performance Measurement Baseline's component budgets (control accounts, planning packages, undistributed budget) exist to preserve accurate, traceable performance history; moving actual variance between them to improve a reported number, rather than through formal, scope-driven change control, is never a valid basis.
corrective_rule: Historical control-account performance must remain visible and traceable; relocating an already-incurred overrun to a different PMB component to hide it violates that traceability requirement.
exam_trap: Baseline-as-performance-lever trap: budget/baseline structure is manipulated (relocated, reclassified, or altered) to mask a real cost-performance problem instead of addressing it.

option_identity: EV=$280,000; CV=$0; CPI=1.00, because actual cost defines earned progress
option_text: EV=$280,000; CV=$0; CPI=1.00, because actual cost defines earned progress
why_wrong: This sets EV equal to AC ($280,000) directly, treating actual cost incurred as if it defined earned progress -- but EV must reflect completed, weighted milestone value (design+procurement=50% of BAC=$250,000), not spending; AC and EV are different quantities that happen to be compared, not substitutes for each other.
governing_concept: Earned Value is the time-phased value of completed, verified physical work (here, completed weighted milestones), never a restatement of what was spent.
corrective_rule: EV must be computed from completed milestone weights x BAC, never set equal to AC.
exam_trap: Three-way EVM-quantity substitution trap: PV, EV, or AC is substituted for one of the other two in a performance measure or baseline-building step.
calculation_path_if_applicable: AC = $280,000 substituted directly for EV (wrong: EV must come from completed milestone weight x BAC = 0.50 x 500,000 = 250,000).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_identity: EV=$350,000; CV=+$70,000; CPI≈1.25, because installation has started
option_text: EV=$350,000; CV=+$70,000; CPI≈1.25, because installation has started
why_wrong: $350,000 (70% of BAC) does not reproduce from any single, defensible weighting error checked: it is not the sum of any two milestone weights (20/30/50 pair sums are 50%, 70%, 80% -- 70% only arises from 20%+50%, which would require BOTH crediting installation's full weight merely for starting AND omitting procurement's already-complete 30%, a compound rather than single error). CV(+70,000) and CPI(1.25) are internally consistent with EV=350,000 and the given AC=280,000, but no single confirmed calculation path was found for the 350,000 figure itself.
governing_concept: Weighted-milestone earned value credits ONLY the weights of milestones that are actually fully complete; design (20%) and procurement (30%) are complete here, so EV = (0.20+0.30) x BAC = 0.50 x 500,000 = 250,000 -- installation (50%) earns nothing until it too is fully complete.
corrective_rule: Sum only the weights of FULLY completed milestones and multiply by BAC; a started-but-unfinished milestone (installation here) contributes zero credit under this technique.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: Checked: 20%+30%=50% (=EV_correct); 20%+50%=70% (requires two simultaneous errors, not one); 30%+50%=80%; no single-step misapplication of the milestone weights lands on 70% exactly.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_identity: EV=$500,000; CV=+$220,000; CPI≈1.79, because all scope is authorized
option_text: EV=$500,000; CV=+$220,000; CPI≈1.79, because all scope is authorized
why_wrong: This credits the full BAC ($500,000) as earned because all scope is authorized -- but authorization is not completion; installation (50% of the weight) has not finished, so its value is not yet earned regardless of whether the work package as a whole is authorized to proceed.
governing_concept: Earned value must be grounded in verified physical accomplishment (completed milestones), not in whether scope has been authorized to begin.
corrective_rule: Authorization to perform work is a precondition for earning value, not a substitute for the completion evidence that actually earns it.
exam_trap: EV-independent-of-physical-progress trap: reported EV is accepted despite a material, unreconciled gap from verified physical progress (here: authorized scope mistaken for completed scope).
calculation_path_if_applicable: 100% x $500,000 = $500,000 (wrong: treats authorized-but-incomplete scope as fully earned).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_identity: Approximately 1.20
option_text: Approximately 1.20
why_wrong: This is (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC) = 6/5 = 1.20 -- the standard TCPI-to-BAC formula, which answers 'what efficiency is needed to recover to the ORIGINAL budget,' not the question actually asked (what efficiency is needed to finish at the APPROVED $12.0M forecast).
governing_concept: The required-efficiency target must use the actual target total (the approved EAC here, not the original BAC) in its denominator: (BAC-EV)/(target-AC).
corrective_rule: Substituting BAC for the approved EAC in the denominator answers a different question (recovery to original budget) than the one posed (efficiency needed to hit the approved forecast).
exam_trap: Wrong-target-efficiency trap: a TCPI-family ratio is computed against the wrong target (e.g., recovery to original BAC, or current historical CPI) instead of the specific required forward efficiency the question asks for.
calculation_path_if_applicable: (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC) = (10-4)/(10-5) = 6/5 = 1.20 (wrong target: original BAC instead of the approved $12.0M EAC).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_text: Approximately 0.80

governing_concept: An EAC method (or a decision to keep using BAC as the forecast) is only valid when the continuing-performance assumption it embeds actually matches the performance data and scenario given.
corrective_rule: The current CPI describes past performance; the required TCPI-style ratio must be computed from the remaining work and remaining approved budget, not read directly off the historical index.
exam_trap: Stale-assumption trap: an EAC method (or BAC-as-forecast) whose embedded continuing-performance assumption contradicts the CPI/trend data actually stated.

option_text: Approximately 1.00
why_wrong: This assumes parity (breakeven, no adjustment needed) without computing the actual required efficiency from the remaining budgeted work and remaining approved spending -- an unstated, unjustified assumption rather than a derived value.
governing_concept: An EAC method (or a decision to keep using BAC as the forecast) is only valid when the continuing-performance assumption it embeds actually matches the performance data and scenario given.

option_identity: Deterministic, unit-cost takeoff from completed drawings
option_text: Deterministic, unit-cost takeoff from completed drawings
why_wrong: Deterministic unit-cost takeoff is the methodology tied to Class 2/1 (30-100% project definition), where completed/near-complete drawings exist. A Class 5 estimate (0-2% definition) is prepared before such drawings exist, so this method cannot be the correct approach for the scenario described.
governing_concept: Per the AACE Cost Estimate Classification Matrix (Fig.9.1/9.2), estimating methodology is a secondary characteristic driven by the level of project definition: Class 5 = stochastic (factors/judgment); Class 2-1 = primarily/fully deterministic.
corrective_rule: Match the methodology column to the class row in the classification matrix — never assume 'more detailed methodology' is always safer or more correct.
exam_trap: Classic 'more rigor is always better' trap: choosing the most detailed-sounding method regardless of whether the stated scope-definition level actually supports it.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)
notes: Distractor names a real, defined methodology (Class 1/2) but pairs it with the wrong class.

option_identity: Primarily deterministic with some stochastic elements
option_text: Primarily deterministic with some stochastic elements
why_wrong: This phrase is the Fig.9.1 methodology description for Class 2 (30-75% project definition), not Class 5. At 0-2% definition there is no meaningful deterministic component available yet.
governing_concept: Fig.9.1 assigns 'Primarily deterministic' methodology specifically to the Class 2 row; Class 5's methodology cell reads 'Stochastic (factors and/or models) or judgment.'
corrective_rule: Recite the matrix row-by-row from memory only loosely — instead re-derive: lower class number = more definition = more deterministic content.
exam_trap: The option is a real matrix cell text lifted from a neighboring class row, testing whether the candidate actually maps text to the correct class rather than pattern-matching plausible-sounding wording.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)
notes: Directly the Class 2 description per Fig.9.1.

option_identity: A vendor-quoted, line-item bid estimate
option_text: A vendor-quoted, line-item bid estimate
why_wrong: A firm, line-item vendor bid requires a defined, biddable scope, which corresponds to Class 2/1 (control or bid/tender end usage), not the 0-2% definition level of a Class 5 screening estimate.
governing_concept: Fig.9.1's 'end usage' column ties bid/tender estimates to Class 2 and Class 1, far above the definition level available for a Class 5 feasibility screen.
corrective_rule: Ask what design/procurement information the scenario actually says exists before assuming a bid-based method is available.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: The identity of the organization preparing it
option_text: The identity of the organization preparing it
why_wrong: RP 17R-97 does not list preparer identity as any of the five classification characteristics (definition, end usage, methodology, accuracy, effort); it is not a driver of class at all.
governing_concept: The level of project definition is the primary, driving characteristic of estimate class; the other four AACE-listed characteristics are secondary and follow from it. Who prepares the estimate (owner vs. contractor) is a separate organizational fact.
corrective_rule: If an option names something not on AACE's five-characteristic list, it cannot be the primary driver.
exam_trap: Exam writers often substitute a plausible-sounding organizational or business fact (preparer, software, dollar value) for the one AACE-defined primary characteristic.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: The dollar value of the project
option_text: The dollar value of the project
why_wrong: Project dollar value is not one of RP 17R-97's five classification characteristics and does not by itself determine an estimate's class; a small project and a large project can both require a Class 5 estimate at 0-2% definition.
governing_concept: The level of project definition (design/scope maturity), not project size or cost, is the primary/driving characteristic per AACE RP 17R-97.
corrective_rule: Class number tracks how much scope/design information exists, not how big or expensive the project is.
exam_trap: Conflating estimate class with project scale is a common real-world and exam misconception.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: The estimating software used
option_text: The estimating software used
why_wrong: The estimating tool/software used to prepare an estimate is not one of RP 17R-97's five classification characteristics and has no defined role in setting class.
governing_concept: Class is set by the maturity of project definition available, independent of which software or calculation tool is used to process that information.
corrective_rule: Software is a preparation tool, not a classification criterion — see also the separate 'Estimating Resources' discussion of software's limited role.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: Wider accuracy range, higher preparation effort
option_text: Wider accuracy range, higher preparation effort
why_wrong: This option gets the accuracy-range direction backwards: Fig.9.1 shows a Class 1 estimate's expected accuracy index at 1 (narrowest) versus 4-20 for Class 5, so Class 1 is narrower, not wider, even though it correctly identifies that preparation effort is higher.
governing_concept: As class number decreases from 5 toward 1 (more project definition), Fig.9.1 shows expected accuracy range narrowing (smaller index) while preparation effort increases (larger index) — the two secondary characteristics move in opposite numeric directions.
corrective_rule: Narrower class number = narrower (better) accuracy AND higher effort — accuracy and effort are inversely related to class number, not to each other.

option_text: USD 10.70 million
why_wrong: This value is close to but not exactly reproducible from the given inputs (12.00 x (250/300)^0.65 = 10.66); it lies in the range produced by small exponent perturbations (e.g., using 0.62-0.63 instead of 0.65) or intermediate rounding of the capacity ratio, none of which is a single, clean, uniquely identifiable substitution error.

option_identity: USD 10.00 million
option_text: USD 10.00 million
why_wrong: This value results from applying the capacity ratio linearly (treating the exponent as 1) instead of raising it to the 0.65 power, i.e. assuming cost scales directly with capacity rather than with economies of scale.
governing_concept: Capacity-factor scaling is explicitly non-linear: cost scales with capacity raised to an exponent typically between 0.5 and 0.85, not one-for-one with capacity.
corrective_rule: If your answer equals a simple pro-rata (linear) scaling of the known cost, you have dropped the exponent — re-check that the ratio was actually raised to the power e.
exam_trap: Classic capacity-factor trap: forgetting that the whole point of the method is the non-linear (economies-of-scale) relationship, and reverting to simple proportion.
calculation_path_if_applicable: 12.00 x (250/300) = 10.00 (linear scaling, exponent omitted/treated as 1.0).

option_text: Management reserve

option_text: SAR 2.67 million
why_wrong: This value results from inverting the index ratio — using historical index/current index (200/300) instead of current index/historical index (300/200) — which produces a decrease when the index actually rose.
governing_concept: The correct ratio for adjusting a historical cost forward in time is (current/new index) over (historical/old index); inverting it effectively deflates rather than escalates the cost.
corrective_rule: Current index goes on top (numerator), historical/base index goes on the bottom (denominator) — never the reverse — when adjusting an old cost to a new basis.

why_wrong: Preferring the older, already-approved estimate ignores the reconciliation step entirely and substitutes prior approval status for actual investigation of what changed and why — approval status is not evidence that the older number is still correct.
governing_concept: Reconciliation exists precisely because scope, pricing, and risk understanding evolve between estimate versions; the newer estimate may be more accurate, and only driver-level reconciliation can tell which is right.
corrective_rule: 'Already approved' is a procedural fact about the old estimate, not evidence about which estimate is currently more accurate.

governing_concept: Reconciliation requires isolating individual drivers of change rather than applying an undifferentiated across-the-board adjustment to force the total back toward a prior value.
corrective_rule: A flat percentage adjustment to force agreement between two estimates is not reconciliation — it hides rather than explains the difference.

option_identity: Discard quotes that contain exclusions
option_text: Discard quotes that contain exclusions
why_wrong: Discarding a quote with exclusions is unnecessary and wasteful when normalization (identifying and pricing the excluded items) is the standard, textbook-consistent way to make an otherwise usable quote comparable — exclusions are routine in vendor quotes, not disqualifying.
governing_concept: The correct response to a quote with exclusions is scope normalization to the required basis, documenting all additions/exclusions, not rejection of the quote.
corrective_rule: An excluded item is something to price and add during normalization, not a reason to reject an otherwise valid quote.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction)

option_identity: Use each quoted total without adjustment
option_text: Use each quoted total without adjustment
why_wrong: Using the raw quoted totals as-is compares bids on inconsistent scope bases (since this quote excludes freight, taxes, commissioning, and spares while others may not), making any cost comparison invalid without first normalizing to a common required scope.
governing_concept: Valid bid comparison requires each quote to be normalized to the same required scope before totals are compared; using unadjusted totals defeats that requirement entirely.
corrective_rule: Never compare bid totals directly unless you have first confirmed (or normalized to) an identical scope basis across all bidders.
exam_trap: A classic bid-leveling exam trap: comparing headline totals without checking each bidder's stated exclusions.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction)

option_identity: Only after contract award
option_text: Only after contract award
why_wrong: Deferring documentation of a material assumption until after contract award defeats the purpose of the assumption register, which is to support review, traceability, and risk management of the estimate before it is used for the funding/award decision it is meant to inform.
governing_concept: Material assumptions affecting price must be documented in the BOE/assumption register at the time they are made so they can be reviewed and reconciled as part of the estimate's own validation, not retroactively after commitments are already made.
corrective_rule: An assumption must be recorded when it is made, not deferred to a point after the decision it informed has already been taken.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_identity: Nowhere if management knows it
option_text: Nowhere if management knows it
why_wrong: Informal awareness by management is not a substitute for formal documentation; without a written record in the BOE/assumption register, the assumption cannot be traced, reviewed by others, or reconciled in later estimate revisions.
governing_concept: Formal documentation exists precisely so that assumptions are traceable beyond any one individual's or manager's personal knowledge, supporting review by parties who were not part of the original conversation.
corrective_rule: Personal or verbal awareness is not documentation; traceability requires a written record independent of who currently 'knows' the assumption.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_identity: Only in the estimator's private notes
option_text: Only in the estimator's private notes
why_wrong: Private, personal notes are not accessible to reviewers, engineering, project management, or later estimators, defeating the traceability and shared-review purpose that formal BOE/assumption-register documentation is meant to serve for a material, price-affecting assumption.
governing_concept: Material assumptions must be captured in the formal, shared BOE/assumption register and carried into risk/reconciliation records — not kept in a location only the original estimator can access.
corrective_rule: If only one person can find the documentation, it isn't serving its traceability purpose.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_identity: Delete superseded assumptions after each approved revision to avoid confusion
option_text: Delete superseded assumptions after each approved revision to avoid confusion
why_wrong: Deleting superseded assumptions destroys exactly the historical record an audit trail exists to preserve; a reviewer would then be unable to see what changed between versions or why, which is the opposite of preserving traceability.
governing_concept: An audit trail requires dated versions of assumptions to be retained (not deleted) alongside reconciliation logs and approvals, so reviewers can see the full history of what changed.
corrective_rule: 'Superseded' does not mean 'discard' — a proper audit trail keeps prior versions visible, dated, and reconciled, not erased.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_identity: Overwrite previous estimate files after reconciling each approved revision
option_text: Overwrite previous estimate files after reconciling each approved revision
why_wrong: Overwriting removes the prior version entirely, so there is no way for a later reviewer to independently verify the reconciliation that was performed or trace the estimate's evolution — version control requires retaining, not replacing, each dated version.
governing_concept: Preserving an audit trail requires version control (retained dated versions) plus reconciliation logs and approvals — reconciling and then destroying the 'before' version defeats the purpose of the reconciliation record itself.
corrective_rule: Reconciliation must be provable after the fact, which requires keeping both the 'before' and 'after' versions, not just the reconciled result.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_identity: Use informal manual adjustments when the value is too small for formal revision
option_text: Use informal manual adjustments when the value is too small for formal revision
why_wrong: Informal, undocumented manual adjustments — regardless of dollar size — bypass the version control, dated-assumption, and approval-record practices the audit trail depends on, creating an untraceable gap in the estimate's history.
governing_concept: An audit trail's integrity does not depend on materiality thresholds chosen ad hoc by the estimator; formal version control and reconciliation logging are the practices described as preserving traceability.
corrective_rule: There is no 'too small to document' exception described for estimate revisions — informal, undocumented changes break the audit trail regardless of size.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_identity: USD 6.34 million
option_text: USD 6.34 million
why_wrong: This results from dividing (discounting) the base cost by (1.06)^4 instead of multiplying by it — applying the compound factor in the deflating direction instead of the escalating direction.
governing_concept: Escalation projects a cost forward in time, so the compound factor (1+rate)^n must multiply, not divide, the base/today's-price cost.
corrective_rule: Escalation makes future costs larger than today's cost, not smaller — if your escalated answer is below the starting cost, the operation was inverted.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: 8.00 / (1.06)^4 = 8.00 / 1.2625 = 6.34 (compound factor applied as a divisor instead of a multiplier).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.97-98 (index/location normalization within Capacity Factor worked example); AACE RP 28R-03 (Location Factors) and RP 58R-10 (Escalation Estimating), listed in Ch.9 Recommended Reading p.130

option_identity: USD 8.48 million
option_text: USD 8.48 million
why_wrong: This applies the 6% escalation rate for only a single year (8.00 x 1.06) instead of compounding it over the full stated 4-year period.
governing_concept: The scenario specifies 6% compounded annually for 4 years, requiring the (1+rate) factor to be raised to the 4th power, not applied once.
corrective_rule: Always match the exponent in a compounding calculation to the number of periods actually stated in the problem.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: 8.00 x 1.06 = 8.48 (only 1 of the 4 stated years of compounding applied).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.97-98 (index/location normalization within Capacity Factor worked example); AACE RP 28R-03 (Location Factors) and RP 58R-10 (Escalation Estimating), listed in Ch.9 Recommended Reading p.130

option_identity: USD 9.92 million
option_text: USD 9.92 million
why_wrong: This applies simple (linear) interest — 4 years x 6% = 24% added once to the base — instead of compound escalation, where each year's escalation is applied to the prior year's already-escalated balance.
governing_concept: 'Compounded for 4 years' means each period's growth applies to the previous period's escalated value ((1.06)^4), not a single flat percentage equal to rate times number of years.
corrective_rule: Compound growth over n years is (1+rate)^n, not (1 + rate x n) — the two only coincide for very small rates or short periods, and diverge here.
exam_trap: A very common escalation exam trap: substituting simple interest for compound interest when the problem explicitly says 'compounded.'
calculation_path_if_applicable: 8.00 x (1 + 0.06x4) = 8.00 x 1.24 = 9.92 (simple/linear escalation instead of compound).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.97-98 (index/location normalization within Capacity Factor worked example); AACE RP 28R-03 (Location Factors) and RP 58R-10 (Escalation Estimating), listed in Ch.9 Recommended Reading p.130

option_identity: Class number has no relationship to project definition; classes are assigned arbitrarily
option_text: Class number has no relationship to project definition; classes are assigned arbitrarily
why_wrong: This directly contradicts RP 17R-97/18R-97, which define project definition/maturity as the explicit primary, driving characteristic used to assign class number — the relationship is systematic and defined, not arbitrary.
governing_concept: AACE's classification system is built entirely around project definition level as the primary characteristic determining class; class assignment is a structured mapping, not an arbitrary label.
corrective_rule: 'Arbitrary' options that deny a defined, textbook relationship exists are almost always wrong when the relationship is the chapter's central topic.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: Class 1 represents the least mature project definition and the widest typical accuracy range
option_text: Class 1 represents the least mature project definition and the widest typical accuracy range
why_wrong: This reverses the actual relationship: Class 1 (65-100% definition) is the MOST mature, with the NARROWEST typical accuracy range (index 1), while Class 5 (0-2% definition) is the least mature with the widest range (index 4-20).
governing_concept: Fig.9.1/9.2 define Class 5 as least mature/widest range and Class 1 as most mature/narrowest range — the inverse of what this option claims.
corrective_rule: Class 1 = most defined, most accurate; Class 5 = least defined, least accurate — memorize the two endpoints of the scale correctly and in the right direction.
exam_trap: A direct reversal-of-relationship trap for candidates who remember 'Class 1 and Class 5 are opposite ends' but mix up which end is which.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: Class 3 corresponds to a nearly complete design and therefore has a fixed definition percentage across industries
option_text: Class 3 corresponds to a nearly complete design and therefore has a fixed definition percentage across industries
why_wrong: Class 3 corresponds to only 10-40% project definition (budget authorization/control stage), not a 'nearly complete' design, and the text explicitly states percentage ranges vary by industry sector, methodology, and how risk/contingency is addressed rather than being fixed constants.
governing_concept: The generic matrix (Fig.9.1) gives Class 3 as 10-40% definition, and the chapter explicitly warns these ranges are indicative, not universal fixed constants to memorize, and vary by industry-specific supplements like RP 18R-97's process-industry matrix (Fig.9.2).
corrective_rule: Definition-percentage ranges by class are indicative guidance, not fixed universal constants — and Class 3 is a budget-stage, not near-complete-design, estimate.
exam_trap: Combines two errors in one option (wrong percentage-maturity level for Class 3, plus a false 'fixed across industries' absolute claim) — testing whether the candidate catches both.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: A universal constant equal to 0.6 for all facility types
option_text: A universal constant equal to 0.6 for all facility types
why_wrong: The text explicitly describes 0.6 as a fallback default used 'if no other information is available' (the 'six tenth's factor'), not a universal constant; the actual exponent typically ranges from 0.5 to 0.85 and is facility/technology specific, and the text further notes the exponent itself changes across capacity ranges for a given facility.
governing_concept: The capacity-factor exponent e is a project- and industry/technology-specific value best derived from an organization's own historical cost-vs-capacity data; 0.6 is only a last-resort default, not a governing constant.
corrective_rule: 0.6 is a 'if nothing else is available' fallback, not the correct value to use whenever better data exists.
exam_trap: A well-known CCP exam trap: treating the historically famous '0.6 (six-tenths) factor' nickname as if it were the mandated or only correct exponent value.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_identity: Always equal to 1.0, meaning cost scales linearly with capacity
option_text: Always equal to 1.0, meaning cost scales linearly with capacity
why_wrong: The entire premise of the capacity-factor method is a non-linear cost-capacity relationship (typical exponents of 0.5-0.85, reflecting economies of scale); an exponent of 1.0 would make the method pointless, since a linear relationship needs no exponential factor at all, and the text explicitly frames e=1 as only the theoretical endpoint where economies of scale disappear at very large capacities.
governing_concept: Cost-capacity scaling is defined as non-linear for most facility types (exponent typically 0.5-0.85); a value of 1.0 (linear) is described only as the limiting case at the upper bound of a technology's economies of scale, not the general rule.
corrective_rule: If the exponent equaled 1.0 as a rule, the capacity-factor method would collapse into simple proportional scaling — the method's entire value proposition depends on it usually not being 1.0.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_identity: Irrelevant to the estimate as long as Q1 and Q2 are known
option_text: Irrelevant to the estimate as long as Q1 and Q2 are known
why_wrong: The exponent e is the specific term in the formula that determines how much cost changes as capacity changes; knowing only the two capacity values without the exponent provides no way to compute the cost ratio at all, so the exponent cannot be irrelevant.
governing_concept: The capacity-factor formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e requires all three inputs (A, capacity ratio, and e); the exponent directly and materially changes the computed result, as shown by the chapter's own sensitivity example (a wrong exponent producing ~10-12% error).
corrective_rule: A formula's exponent term is never 'irrelevant' if the formula cannot be evaluated without it.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_identity: Significantly reduces the training time needed for new estimating staff
option_text: Significantly reduces the training time needed for new estimating staff
why_wrong: This is the specific expectation the scenario describes and the text directly rejects: the source states plainly that estimating software 'doesn't convert a non-estimator to be an estimator,' meaning it does not substitute for or significantly shorten the training/experience required of estimating staff.
governing_concept: Estimating software is described as a tool to facilitate preparation of estimates by already-trained estimators, and commercial cost databases still require calibration to specific organizational needs — it augments trained estimators rather than replacing the need for their training.
corrective_rule: A tool that facilitates expert work is not the same as a tool that creates the expertise — software assists estimators, it does not manufacture them.
exam_trap: The core misconception the item is built to test directly — mistaking a productivity tool for a substitute for professional training.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.128-129 (Estimating Resources)

option_identity: Primarily useful for conceptual estimates rather than detailed ones
option_text: Primarily useful for conceptual estimates rather than detailed ones
why_wrong: The text discusses estimating software as a general resource that assists in the preparation of estimates broadly, without limiting its usefulness to conceptual estimates; the passage specifically discussed (p.129) concerns training/experience substitution, not a class-based restriction on software utility.
governing_concept: Estimating software is presented as a general productivity and consistency tool applicable across the estimating process, calibrated to organizational needs, not restricted to any one class of estimate.
corrective_rule: The chapter never ties software usefulness to estimate class — do not infer a scope restriction the text does not state.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.128-129 (Estimating Resources)

option_identity: Should be avoided in favor of fully manual estimating methods
option_text: Should be avoided in favor of fully manual estimating methods
why_wrong: This overcorrects the scenario's flawed premise into an opposite absolute: the text frames software as a legitimate, valuable tool ('can enhance the accuracy and consistency of estimates, while reducing the time required') when used properly by trained estimators — it does not recommend avoiding it in favor of manual methods.
governing_concept: Estimating software is described as enhancing accuracy, consistency, and speed for trained estimators, with the caveat that it requires trained users and calibrated databases — not as something to be avoided altogether.
corrective_rule: Correctly rejecting an overstated benefit of a tool does not mean the tool should be discarded entirely — check whether the text recommends avoidance or just tempered, informed use.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.128-129 (Estimating Resources)

option_identity: Escalation estimating
option_text: Escalation estimating
why_wrong: Escalation estimating addresses time/market-based price adjustment of costs, an entirely different activity from counting/quantifying material and labor items off engineering drawings, which is the process described in the question.
governing_concept: Take-off is specifically defined as examining engineering drawings to count and quantify material/labor items, summarized per the project's control structure — a scope-quantification activity, not a price-adjustment activity like escalation.
corrective_rule: Take-off answers 'how much of each item is there'; escalation answers 'how does price change over time' — different questions entirely.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction)

option_identity: Risk analysis
option_text: Risk analysis
why_wrong: Risk analysis is a probabilistic process for understanding the likelihood of overrunning/underrunning an estimate value, unrelated to the mechanical drawing-based quantity-counting activity described in the question.
governing_concept: Take-off is a deterministic quantity-counting process from drawings; risk analysis is a separate, probabilistic activity used to determine contingency, addressed later in the chapter under Contingency and Risk Analysis.
corrective_rule: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction); S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Benchmarking
option_text: Benchmarking
why_wrong: Benchmarking compares estimate metrics/ratios (e.g., cost per unit of capacity) against similar completed projects for validation purposes; it is not the process of counting and quantifying material/labor items from drawings described in the question.
governing_concept: Take-off produces the quantities used to build up a detailed estimate directly from drawings; benchmarking is a separate validation technique comparing derived estimate metrics to historical project data.
corrective_rule: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction); S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_identity: A skewed probability distribution and a normal probability distribution, respectively
option_text: A skewed probability distribution and a normal probability distribution, respectively
why_wrong: This reverses which line item matches which distribution shape: the 50/50 under/overrun case (equal probability on both sides of the point value) is the normal distribution (Fig.9.10), and the 40/60 case (unequal probability) is the skewed one (Fig.9.11) — this option swaps the two labels.
governing_concept: A symmetric (50%/50%) probability split around the point estimate defines a normal distribution; an asymmetric split (e.g., 40%/60%) defines a skewed distribution, per Fig.9.10 and 9.11.
corrective_rule: Equal split = normal; unequal split = skewed — match each percentage pair to its shape in the order given in the question, not reversed.
exam_trap: A straightforward order-reversal trap testing careful reading of which situation (first vs. second) was described as 50/50 vs 40/60.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Both represent normal probability distributions, differing only in scale
option_text: Both represent normal probability distributions, differing only in scale
why_wrong: The two situations have different underlying probability splits (50/50 vs 40/60), which is a difference in distribution shape (symmetric vs. skewed), not merely a difference in scale or magnitude of a shared normal shape.
governing_concept: A distribution is 'normal' specifically because it is symmetric (equal underrun/overrun probability); the 40/60 case is by definition not symmetric and therefore not normal, regardless of scale.
corrective_rule: Symmetry (or its absence) defines distribution shape category; it is not a 'scale' parameter that can vary within one shape while keeping the shape the same.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Both represent skewed distributions, differing only in direction
option_text: Both represent skewed distributions, differing only in direction
why_wrong: A 50%/50% underrun/overrun split has no skew at all (it is symmetric by definition), so it cannot be described as a skewed distribution merely 'in a different direction' from the 40/60 case — one of the two cases is not skewed.
governing_concept: Skew requires an unequal probability split; the 50/50 case is the textbook definition of a normal (unskewed) distribution, not a skewed one with zero direction.
corrective_rule: A 50/50 split is the absence of skew, not a skew 'direction' of its own.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Variability associated with the quantification effort
option_text: Variability associated with the quantification effort
why_wrong: This item is explicitly listed among what contingency IS intended to cover (variability associated with the quantification effort, since design may not be complete enough to determine final quantities), not among the explicitly excluded items.
governing_concept: The chapter's 'items typically covered by contingency' list explicitly names quantification-effort variability as a covered item, distinct from the separately listed excluded items (major scope changes, work stoppages, disasters, excessive unexpected inflation/currency swings).
corrective_rule: Quantification/estimating variability within a defined scope is exactly what contingency is for — it is the opposite of an excluded item.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Labor productivity variability due to weather assumptions
option_text: Labor productivity variability due to weather assumptions
why_wrong: The chapter explicitly lists ordinary weather-driven labor productivity variability among the items contingency IS intended to cover, not among the excluded items — only major unexpected events (not routine weather variation) fall outside contingency's coverage.
governing_concept: 'Items typically covered by contingency' explicitly includes 'weather may vary from that assumed, affecting labor productivity,' distinguishing routine weather variability (covered) from disasters like hurricanes (excluded).
corrective_rule: Ordinary weather variability is covered by contingency; only catastrophic weather events (disasters) are excluded — the distinction is severity/type, not the mere presence of weather.
exam_trap: Tests whether the candidate distinguishes routine weather-driven productivity variance (covered) from the disaster-category exclusion (hurricanes, excluded) — both involve 'weather' but sit on opposite sides of the boundary.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Wage rate variability due to inflationary reasons
option_text: Wage rate variability due to inflationary reasons
why_wrong: The chapter explicitly lists ordinary wage-rate variability 'because of inflationary reasons' among the items contingency IS intended to cover; only excessive, unexpected inflation is separately excluded, not ordinary inflation-driven wage variability.
governing_concept: 'Items typically covered by contingency' explicitly includes wage rate variability from inflationary reasons, changes in crew mix, and market conditions; the excluded-items list instead names 'excessive, unexpected inflation' as a distinct, more extreme category.
corrective_rule: Ordinary/expected inflationary wage drift is covered by contingency; only excessive, unexpected inflation is excluded — do not conflate the two.
exam_trap: Pairs closely with the excluded item's wording ('excessive, unexpected inflation') to test whether the candidate can distinguish ordinary covered inflation effects from the excluded extreme case.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

why_wrong: This is simply the known 1,200-bed hospital's cost carried forward unchanged, with no scaling for the different (1,800-bed) end-product unit count applied at all.
governing_concept: The end-product units method requires deriving a cost-per-unit rate from the known facility and then multiplying by the new facility's unit count; reporting the known facility's raw total skips both steps.
corrective_rule: If your answer exactly equals the known facility's given cost, the scaling calculation was never performed.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: 84,000,000 (known-facility cost reused unchanged for a differently sized facility).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.94-95 (End-Product Units Method); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

why_wrong: This is the correctly derived per-bed rate ($84,000,000/1,200 = $70,000/bed) reported directly as the answer, with the required final step of multiplying by the new facility's 1,800 beds omitted.
governing_concept: The end-product units method has two required steps: derive the unit rate, then multiply by the new quantity; stopping after the first step yields a per-unit rate, not a total project cost.
corrective_rule: Check units: a per-bed rate ($/bed) is not the same quantity as a total project cost ($) — if the answer 'looks like' the intermediate rate, the final multiplication was likely skipped.
exam_trap: A subtle trap because $70,000 (the correct per-unit rate) is scaled up by exactly 1,000x by coincidence of the numbers chosen, making it a very plausible-looking wrong total.
calculation_path_if_applicable: 84,000,000/1,200 = 70,000 (correct unit rate, but reported without multiplying by the new 1,800-bed quantity).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.94-95 (End-Product Units Method)
notes: Downgraded from SPECIFIC_CALCULATION_PATH_VERIFIED on independent review: the unit-rate figure ($70,000/bed) does not numerically reproduce the option ($70,000,000) via a single clean arithmetic operation -- the explanation relies on a units-relabeling narrative rather than exact reproduction.

why_wrong: This results from using 1,000 (not the stated 1,200) as the known facility's bed count when deriving the per-bed rate before multiplying by 1,800 new beds — an incorrect substitution of the base quantity given in the problem.
governing_concept: The known facility's actual stated bed count (1,200) must be used as the denominator when deriving the per-bed rate; substituting a different, unstated base quantity produces a wrong rate and thus a wrong total.
corrective_rule: Always re-verify which numbers in the problem are the 'known/base' values before dividing — do not substitute a number from memory or a similar prior example.
exam_trap: A plausible mis-substitution trap, possibly echoing the chapter's own illustrative hotel example which used a 1,000-unit base for an unrelated scenario.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.94-95 (End-Product Units Method)

why_wrong: This is simply the known 2,400 SM warehouse's cost carried forward unchanged, with no area-based scaling applied for the new, larger (3,100 SM) warehouse at all.
governing_concept: The physical dimensions method requires deriving a cost-per-area rate from the known facility and multiplying by the new facility's area; reporting the known facility's raw total skips both required steps.
corrective_rule: If your answer exactly equals the known facility's given cost, the area-scaling calculation was never performed.

option_text: Bid 1 normalized ≈ $1,200,000, making Bid 1 clearly more competitive than Bid 2

governing_concept: Normalizing Bid 1 to Bid 2's time period requires multiplying by (Index 2/Index 1) = 168.9/150.2; using the raw $1,200,000 figure skips the entire normalization step the question asks for.
corrective_rule: Two bids from different index periods cannot be validly compared until at least one is normalized to the other's time basis.

option_text: Bid 1 normalized ≈ $1,517,000, making Bid 2 clearly more competitive than Bid 1
why_wrong: This results from squaring the index ratio (applying it twice, (168.9/150.2)^2) instead of applying it once, effectively double-compounding the escalation adjustment.
governing_concept: Normalizing a single historical value to a new index period requires multiplying by the index ratio exactly once: Normalized Bid 1 = Bid 1 x (Index 2/Index 1).
corrective_rule: An index-ratio normalization is applied once, not compounded/squared — confirm the ratio appears in the calculation exactly one time.

option_text: Bid 1 normalized ≈ $1,350,000, but Bid 2 is still cheaper on an absolute, unadjusted basis
why_wrong: This option arrives at approximately the correct normalized figure but then draws an internally inconsistent conclusion by reverting to an 'absolute, unadjusted basis' comparison — once normalization has been performed to place both bids on the same time basis, comparing on an unadjusted basis afterward contradicts the normalization just completed and misreads what the normalized result actually shows (the two bids are essentially equivalent, not one cheaper than the other).
governing_concept: Once Bid 1 is normalized to Bid 2's index period, the comparison must be made using that normalized figure, not by reverting to the original unadjusted total for one of the two bids.
corrective_rule: After normalizing for a valid comparison, do not selectively fall back to unadjusted figures to reach a conclusion — that reintroduces the very inconsistency normalization was meant to remove.
exam_trap: A reasoning-consistency trap: the numeric normalization is nearly right, but the stated conclusion contradicts its own premise.

option_text: Combine the three final costs into one average without normalizing capacity and execution year.

governing_concept: Developing an analogous data set (Blueprint 1.B) requires normalizing comparable projects for scope, capacity, location, and time differences before use — simple averaging of raw totals skips this required step.

option_text: Discard the historical projects because none is identical to the proposed plant.
why_wrong: Requiring identical (not merely comparable/normalizable) projects is an unrealistically strict standard; the entire purpose of analogous/normalization techniques is to make usefully similar — not identical — historical projects comparable through adjustment, not to discard all non-identical data.
governing_concept: Analogous data development is specifically the practice of normalizing non-identical but comparable historical projects for capacity, location, and time differences so they can validly inform a new estimate.

option_text: Select the project with the closest total cost and use its value without normalization.

governing_concept: A project's total cost alone does not establish it as a valid analog; normalization for capacity, location, and time differences is required regardless of how numerically close a raw total happens to be.

option_text: Report a single total without documenting the scope basis because the estimate is preliminary.

corrective_rule: 'Preliminary' describes the estimate's maturity, not an exemption from documenting what it is based on.

option_identity: Delay any estimate until all quantities can be measured from final design documents.
option_text: Delay any estimate until all quantities can be measured from final design documents.
why_wrong: Refusing to provide any estimate until full design definition exists misapplies the classification framework, which exists precisely so that conceptual (Class 5/4) methods can serve early screening decisions using limited but known major functional quantities — the scenario explicitly states the definition available, not that no estimate is possible.
governing_concept: Conceptual estimating methods (capacity factor, parametric, end-product units) are specifically designed to produce usable screening estimates at low project definition using available major quantities; withholding all estimating output until final design is a misuse of, not adherence to, the classification system.
corrective_rule: A low-definition scenario calls for a low-definition (Class 5/4) method, not a refusal to estimate at all.
exam_trap: A subtle trap that sounds like conservative rigor but actually misapplies the classification system's purpose — every definition level has an appropriate estimate class, including the earliest.

option_identity: Perform a detailed unit-cost takeoff as though issued-for-construction drawings were available.
option_text: Perform a detailed unit-cost takeoff as though issued-for-construction drawings were available.
why_wrong: A detailed unit-cost takeoff requires the deliverables (issued-for-construction drawings) that the scenario explicitly says do not exist ('limited design definition'); performing this deterministic technique as if such drawings existed is a fabrication of inputs the method requires, not a legitimate summary-level estimate.
governing_concept: Take-off is defined as quantifying items directly from engineering drawings; a deterministic take-off cannot be validly performed when the required drawings do not yet exist, regardless of how the estimator proceeds.
corrective_rule: A detailed takeoff presupposes detailed drawings — it cannot be substituted for a conceptual method just by 'pretending' they exist.

option_identity: Compare the estimate with the budget and approve it whenever the totals are close.
option_text: Compare the estimate with the budget and approve it whenever the totals are close.
why_wrong: Approving an estimate solely because its bottom-line total is close to budget substitutes a top-line variance check for the substantive review the chapter describes — checking math, scope completeness, quantities, rates, productivity, indirects, and reconciling to the basis — any of which could be materially wrong even while the total happens to be close to budget.
governing_concept: A rigorous estimate review examines the estimate's underlying content (scope, quantities, rates, productivity, indirects, assumptions, exclusions, arithmetic) and reconciles it to its basis, independent of how the resulting total compares to a target budget.
corrective_rule: A total that happens to match budget is not evidence the underlying estimate content is correct — the review must verify the content itself.
exam_trap: A common real-world and exam shortcut: treating budget proximity as a proxy for estimate quality.

option_identity: Check vendor quotations and accept labor productivity and indirect-cost inputs from the estimating team without separate validation.
option_text: Check vendor quotations and accept labor productivity and indirect-cost inputs from the estimating team without separate validation.
why_wrong: Validating only vendor quotations while accepting the estimating team's own productivity and indirect-cost inputs without independent check leaves exactly the inputs most subject to estimator judgment and assumption unverified, contrary to the review's purpose of independently examining all major cost-driving inputs.
governing_concept: A complete detailed-estimate review examines productivity and indirect-cost inputs, not just vendor quotations, as part of verifying scope completeness, rates, and assumptions before reconciliation and approval.
corrective_rule: Partial review (only the inputs that are easiest to check, like vendor quotes) is not equivalent to a complete review of all material cost drivers.

option_identity: Use the approved budget as the primary review test and investigate detailed inputs when the total variance appears material.
option_text: Use the approved budget as the primary review test and investigate detailed inputs when the total variance appears material.
why_wrong: Making budget-variance the primary test and only investigating details when variance looks material means an estimate with compensating errors (some inputs too high, others too low, netting to a small total variance) would pass review unexamined, contrary to the chapter's description of a review that always examines the estimate's underlying content.
governing_concept: The chapter's estimate review process (math check, BOE review, engineering review, cost review, validation/benchmarking, reconciliation) is a standard sequence applied regardless of how the total compares to budget, not a variance-triggered exception process.
corrective_rule: Budget-variance-triggered review can miss offsetting errors that never produce a material total variance — the underlying content must be checked regardless.

option_identity: Use detailed crew-based unit rates even though the required scope quantities are not yet defined.
option_text: Use detailed crew-based unit rates even though the required scope quantities are not yet defined.
why_wrong: Detailed crew-based unit rates require defined quantities to apply the rates to; the scenario explicitly states the concept is at very low definition, so this deterministic method's required inputs (defined quantities) do not exist, making it inapplicable regardless of how it is attempted.
governing_concept: Deterministic (crew-based unit-rate) methods require quantified scope; at very low project definition, conceptual methods (capacity factor, parametric, judgment) are the textbook-appropriate approach for a ROM estimate instead.
corrective_rule: Unit rates need quantities to multiply against — without defined quantities, a deterministic crew-rate method has no valid input to work from.

option_identity: Treat the ROM as a control estimate once management selects the concept.
option_text: Treat the ROM as a control estimate once management selects the concept.
why_wrong: An estimate's class is fixed by the level of project definition available when it was prepared, not by a subsequent management decision; concept selection does not itself add the project definition needed to upgrade a ROM/Class 5 estimate to a control-grade (Class 2) estimate without re-preparing it to that higher class's required definition and methodology.
governing_concept: Class and accuracy range are tied to the level of project definition used to prepare the estimate; promoting a low-definition ROM to serve as a control estimate silently understates the true uncertainty a control estimate is expected to have.
corrective_rule: Selecting a concept is a decision about the project, not an act of adding the scope definition an estimate needs to change class.
exam_trap: A genuine and consequential real-world CCP exam trap: silently repurposing an early estimate for a later, higher-stakes control use without re-estimating it to the required class.

option_identity: Present a point estimate to the nearest dollar so management can compare alternatives precisely.
option_text: Present a point estimate to the nearest dollar so management can compare alternatives precisely.
why_wrong: Presenting a ROM (Class 5) estimate to the nearest dollar implies a level of precision the underlying low-definition methodology and wide typical accuracy range (roughly -20/-50% to +30/+100% per Fig.9.2) cannot actually support, misleading the reader about the estimate's true uncertainty.
governing_concept: Estimate presentation and precision should reflect the estimate's actual class-based accuracy range; a ROM's value and any comparison based on it should be presented with its stated uncertainty, not as a falsely precise single figure.
corrective_rule: The number of significant digits presented should never exceed what the estimate's underlying accuracy range can actually support.

option_identity: Reconstruct the missing basis after project execution when actual costs are known.
option_text: Reconstruct the missing basis after project execution when actual costs are known.
why_wrong: Deferring basis documentation until after execution defeats the purpose of verifying the BOE before approval — the reviewer's job is to confirm the basis exists and is traceable at the time of approval, not to permit approval now and reconstruct justification later once actual costs are already known (which would also risk the reconstruction being biased toward matching the known outcome).
governing_concept: Verifying the BOE (Blueprint 1.F) means confirming scope, assumptions, exclusions, data date, methodology, and pricing inputs are documented and traceable before the estimate is approved and used.
corrective_rule: A missing basis must be supplied before approval, not reconstructed retroactively after the numbers it was supposed to justify have already been acted on.

option_text: Use the estimate class designation as a substitute for documenting scope and assumptions.
why_wrong: An estimate class designation (e.g., 'Class 3') only indicates the general maturity level and typical characteristics of an estimate; it does not itself document the project-specific scope, assumptions, exclusions, or pricing inputs that the BOE is specifically required to capture for that particular estimate.
governing_concept: The BOE's design/planning/cost/risk-basis sections document project-specific scope, assumptions, and methodology; the estimate class is a separate classification label and cannot substitute for that project-specific documentation.
corrective_rule: A class label tells you the estimate's general maturity category; it does not tell you what this specific estimate actually assumed or excluded.

governing_concept: Verifying the BOE means confirming scope, assumptions, exclusions, data date, methodology, and pricing inputs are documented and traceable, independent of whether the resulting total happens to fall within a target budget.

option_text: Average the two totals so neither estimating team is favored.
why_wrong: Averaging the two totals is a politically neutral but analytically empty response — it does not identify which specific inputs (quantities, rates, productivity, indirects, allowances, assumptions) differ between the estimates or which estimate is more defensible, which is what analyzing a material difference actually requires.
governing_concept: Analyzing a material difference between two estimates for the same scope requires comparing the specific input drivers (quantities, rates, productivity, indirects, allowances, assumptions) to isolate the cause, not averaging the bottom-line totals.
corrective_rule: An average of two totals explains nothing about why they differ — it manufactures a third number with no analytical basis.

option_text: Compare only contingency percentages because normalized dates remove other meaningful differences.
why_wrong: Normalizing to a common date only removes time/escalation-driven differences; it does nothing to reconcile quantities, unit rates, productivity, indirects, or allowances, so restricting the analysis to contingency percentages ignores the other categories of drivers the chapter identifies as sources of estimate difference.
governing_concept: Escalation is only one of several driver categories (scope, quantities, rates, assumptions, escalation, risk) that must be reconciled between estimate versions; normalizing for date does not eliminate the need to also compare the other drivers.

option_identity: Select the lower estimate because both were prepared for the same scope.
option_text: Select the lower estimate because both were prepared for the same scope.
why_wrong: Same nominal scope does not guarantee the same rates, productivity assumptions, indirects, or allowances were used; selecting the lower total without analyzing these drivers risks unknowingly adopting an estimate that is lower because it is less complete or uses unrealistic assumptions, not because it is more accurate.
governing_concept: 'Same scope' addresses only one input category; a valid comparison still requires isolating differences in quantities, unit rates, productivity, indirects, allowances, and assumptions before concluding which estimate is more credible.
corrective_rule: A lower number is not automatically a better number — it must be explained by specific, defensible input differences.
exam_trap: A common cost-suppression trap: assuming the cheaper of two same-scope estimates must be the more accurate one.

option_text: Use the total variance as the cost driver without decomposing its causes.

option_text: Identify the largest cost account as the driver because it contributes the most dollars.

governing_concept: Cost-driver evaluation requires isolating which specific quantity, rate, productivity, escalation, scope, or execution factors actually changed relative to plan, not simply ranking accounts by absolute dollar magnitude.

option_text: Attribute the increase to inflation because material prices changed during the project.

governing_concept: Evaluating cost drivers requires separating and evaluating all relevant categories (quantity, rate, productivity, escalation, scope, execution), not defaulting to a single plausible-sounding cause (inflation) without checking the others.

option_text: Retain accounting transactions without scope, quantity, schedule, or change context.

option_identity: 2 days
option_text: 2 days
why_wrong: 2 days = EF-LS = 16-14. This crosses an early date (EF) with a late date (LS) from the opposite end of the activity instead of pairing LS with ES (or LF with EF) as the Total Float formula requires.
governing_concept: Total Float = LS - ES = LF - EF, using the SAME date-type pairing (both early dates or both late dates) on each side; float is not any arbitrary subtraction of two of the four schedule dates.
corrective_rule: Only subtract ES from LS, or EF from LF -- never cross an early date with a late date from the opposite end.
exam_trap: Mixing an early-side date with a late-side date from the opposite end of the activity (EF-LS or LS-EF) instead of pairing same-end dates.
calculation_path_if_applicable: TF(wrong) = EF - LS = 16 - 14 = 2 days (invalid pairing; correct TF = LS-ES = LF-EF = 4 days)

option_identity: 6 days
option_text: 6 days
why_wrong: 6 days = EF-ES = 16-10, which is the activity's own duration (its early-date span), not its float. Because TF is equal on both ends here (LS-ES=LF-EF=4), this also equals LF-LS, but both routes reduce to the same underlying error: reporting the activity's duration instead of its float.
governing_concept: Total Float = LS - ES = LF - EF, using the SAME date-type pairing (both early dates or both late dates) on each side; float is not any arbitrary subtraction of two of the four schedule dates.
