governing_concept: CPI and SPI are independent measures with different denominators (AC vs. PV); one cannot be inferred from the other's value.
corrective_rule: Never infer schedule status from a cost index's value, or vice versa -- check which denominator (AC or PV) the index actually uses.
exam_trap: A CPI below 1.0 being reinterpreted as a schedule-direction statement (and even flipped to 'ahead') tests whether the candidate conflates the two axes of EVM performance.

option_identity: The account is forecast to finish on budget if schedule performance holds
option_text: The account is forecast to finish on budget if schedule performance holds
why_wrong: CPI's unfavorable cost signal (0.85) implies a likely cost overrun on its own, independent of schedule; making the cost forecast contingent on 'schedule performance holding' incorrectly treats SPI as a precondition for CPI's validity, conflating the two independent indices.
governing_concept: CPI and SPI are independent measures; CPI alone (if it persists) drives cost forecasts such as EAC=BAC/CPI regardless of what SPI shows.
corrective_rule: A cost-efficiency signal stands on its own -- it does not need a schedule condition to 'hold' before it is meaningful.
exam_trap: Distractors that make one EVM figure's conclusion conditional on another figure's future behavior are testing whether the candidate treats CPI and SPI as genuinely independent.

option_identity: SV = +$3,000, SPI = 1.11 (ahead of schedule)
option_text: SV = +$3,000, SPI = 1.11 (ahead of schedule)
why_wrong: SV's subtraction order is reversed (PV-EV = $30,000-$27,000 = +$3,000 instead of EV-PV), and SPI is the reciprocal PV/EV = 1.11; both errors point the same (wrong) direction, so the pair is internally consistent but wrong.
governing_concept: SV = EV-PV (Eq. 19.13) and SPI = EV/PV (Eq. 19.14); earned value is always first/on top in both formulas.
corrective_rule: Keep EV first in both formulas: SV = EV-PV (never PV-EV) and SPI = EV/PV (never PV/EV).
exam_trap: A fully self-consistent but fully backwards SV/SPI pair is a harder trap than a single-figure error because both numbers 'agree' with each other.
calculation_path_if_applicable: SV shown = 30,000-27,000 = +3,000 (PV-EV, reversed from correct EV-PV=-3,000). SPI shown = 30,000/27,000 = 1.11 (reciprocal of correct 0.90).

option_identity: SV = -$3,000, SPI = 1.11 (behind schedule)
option_text: SV = -$3,000, SPI = 1.11 (behind schedule)
why_wrong: SV is correctly calculated (EV-PV = -$3,000), but SPI shown (1.11) is the reciprocal PV/EV instead of EV/PV -- and the option mislabels this reciprocal 'behind schedule' even though an index above 1.0 would normally read as ahead, which is internally inconsistent.
governing_concept: SPI = EV/PV (Eq. 19.14); earned value is always the numerator, and a value at or above 1.0 is favorable/ahead.
corrective_rule: Always put earned value on top: SPI = EV/PV, never PV/EV.
exam_trap: A correct SV paired with a swapped-operand SPI catches candidates who verify only one of two paired figures.
calculation_path_if_applicable: SV = 27,000-30,000 = -3,000 (correct). SPI shown = 30,000/27,000 = 1.11 (reciprocal of correct EV/PV = 0.90).

option_identity: SV = $0, SPI = 1.00 (on schedule)
option_text: SV = $0, SPI = 1.00 (on schedule)
why_wrong: SV of exactly $0 and SPI of exactly 1.00 do not follow from EV=$27,000 and PV=$30,000 under the correct formula, nor from any single identifiable operand substitution; this option appears to assume EV=PV (no schedule deviation) without any actual computation from the given figures.
governing_concept: SV = EV-PV and SPI = EV/PV (Eqs. 19.13-19.14); with EV != PV as given, neither can legitimately equal zero/1.00.
corrective_rule: Always compute SV/SPI from the actual EV and PV given -- never assume 'on schedule' as a default.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
notes: Considered whether this reflects the LOE convention (EV defined to equal PV, making SV always 0), but the stem gives no indication this is Level-of-Effort work, so that specific origin could not be confirmed; multiple plausible (unverifiable) origins -> downgraded per rigor rule 3.

why_wrong: $200,000 is simply the original BAC restated unchanged; it ignores both the $100,000 already spent and the required 'remaining budgeted work' adjustment that Method 1's own formula (AC + (BAC-EV)) explicitly requires.
governing_concept: EAC Method 1 = AC to-date + (Budget - EV) (Eq. 19.6); it is never just the original budget re-stated, since actual cost incurred must always be part of any EAC.
corrective_rule: An EAC can never simply equal the untouched original BAC once actual cost and earned value data exist -- always run the formula.
exam_trap: Restating BAC as the 'forecast' tests whether the candidate has actually computed a forecast versus just recognizing a familiar-looking number.
notes: New Ch.19 code: no Ch.14 code specifically covers an EAC forecast that simply repeats BAC with zero adjustment (distinct from EAC_ASSUMPTION_MISMATCH, which concerns choosing the wrong VALID method, and from EAC_FORMULA_OPERATION_ERROR, which concerns a wrong arithmetic operation on real operands). Also produced in 19-21's $9,600 option, confirming reuse value.

why_wrong: $180,000 = AC + EV ($100,000 + $80,000), substituting earned value directly for the 'remaining budgeted work' term (BAC-EV=$120,000) that Method 1's formula actually calls for -- the addition itself is performed correctly, but the wrong second operand is used.
governing_concept: EAC Method 1 = AC + (BAC - EV) (Eq. 19.6); the second addend must be the budgeted value of work still remaining, not the value already earned.
corrective_rule: Before adding, always compute the remaining-work term as BAC minus EV -- never add EV itself.
exam_trap: Adding AC+EV instead of AC+(BAC-EV) produces a plausible-looking dollar figure that is actually the mirror-image mistake of the correct remaining-work term.

why_wrong: $250,000 = BAC/CPI = $200,000/0.80, which is the Method 2 answer (assumes the current 0.80 CPI continues for all remaining work); the question specifically asks for Method 1 (remaining work proceeds at the budgeted rate, CPI=1 going forward), an entirely different continuing-performance assumption.
governing_concept: Method 1 assumes CPI=1 for remaining work (Eq. 19.6: AC+(BAC-EV)); Method 2 assumes the CPI observed to-date (0.80) persists (Eq. 19.7: BAC/CPI). The two embed different, mutually exclusive assumptions about future performance.
corrective_rule: Match the EAC formula to the assumption actually named in the question -- 'proceeds at budgeted rate' means Method 1, 'performance continues' means Method 2.
exam_trap: Swapping in the Method 2 (BAC/CPI) answer when Method 1 is explicitly requested is one of the most common EAC-family traps on the exam.
calculation_path_if_applicable: CPI = 80,000/100,000 = 0.80. BAC/CPI = 200,000/0.80 = 250,000 (Method 2, not the Method 1 requested).

why_wrong: $220,000 = AC+(BAC-EV) = $100,000+$120,000, the Method 1 answer (assumes remaining work proceeds at the budgeted rate, CPI=1 going forward); the question specifically asks for Method 2, which assumes the current 0.80 CPI continues -- a different continuing-performance assumption.
governing_concept: Method 2 assumes the CPI observed to-date continues for all remaining work: EAC = BAC/CPI (Eq. 19.7), distinct from Method 1's budget-rate assumption (Eq. 19.6).
corrective_rule: Match the EAC formula to the stated assumption -- 'performance to-date continues' means Method 2 (BAC/CPI), not Method 1 (AC+(BAC-EV)).
exam_trap: Swapping in the Method 1 answer when Method 2 is explicitly requested is one of the most common EAC-family traps on the exam.
calculation_path_if_applicable: AC + (BAC-EV) = 100,000 + (200,000-80,000) = 220,000 (Method 1, not the Method 2 requested).

why_wrong: $160,000 = BAC x CPI ($200,000 x 0.80), multiplying instead of dividing; Method 2's formula specifically calls for BAC divided by CPI, and multiplying produces a value below BAC even though CPI<1.0 signals a cost OVERRUN, which is directionally backwards.
governing_concept: EAC Method 2 = BAC/CPI (Eq. 19.7); division, not multiplication, is the required operation.
corrective_rule: Divide BAC by CPI, never multiply -- multiplying with an unfavorable CPI (<1.0) would nonsensically forecast a cost UNDER the budget.
exam_trap: This operand-correct, operation-wrong distractor produces a number that moves in the wrong direction relative to the known unfavorable CPI, which is a useful sanity check.

why_wrong: $180,000 = AC + EV ($100,000 + $80,000), the same 'earned value substituted for remaining budgeted work' operand error seen in the Method 1 version of this scenario (19-5's $180,000 distractor) -- it does not correspond to Method 2's BAC/CPI formula at all.
governing_concept: EAC Method 2 = BAC/CPI (Eq. 19.7), a ratio, not a sum of AC and EV.
corrective_rule: Method 2 is a division of budget by an index -- never an addition of actual cost and earned value.
exam_trap: This value recurs verbatim from the Method 1 scenario, testing whether candidates recognize it doesn't belong to either legitimate EAC formula for Method 2.
calculation_path_if_applicable: AC + EV = 100,000 + 80,000 = 180,000 (no valid EAC formula produces this figure for Method 2).

option_identity: UCI = 1.08; unit rate performance is favorable (below budget rate)
option_text: UCI = 1.08; unit rate performance is favorable (below budget rate)
why_wrong: 1.08 = Actual $/Credit $ ($6,500/$6,000), the reciprocal of the correctly defined UCI = Credit$/Actual$; with numerator and denominator reversed, both the value and the favorable/unfavorable read are inverted from the true 0.92 (unfavorable).
governing_concept: UCI = Credit$/Actual$ (Eq. 19.9), where Credit$ = Actual Qty x Budget Unit Cost (Eq. 19.8a); credit dollars are always the numerator.
corrective_rule: Always put credit dollars (actual quantity valued at the BUDGET rate) on top: UCI = Credit$/Actual$, never the reverse.
exam_trap: A reciprocal UCI value flips both the number and its favorable/unfavorable label together, so checking only 'does the label match the number's direction' will not catch this trap.

option_identity: UCI = 0.92; the account is behind schedule
option_text: UCI = 0.92; the account is behind schedule
why_wrong: The 0.92 value is the correctly computed UCI, but UCI measures unit-rate (cost) performance in isolation from quantity effects -- it carries no schedule information; schedule status is SPI's job and would require BCWS data not given in this problem.
governing_concept: UCI is the ratio of Credit$ to Actual$ (Eq. 19.9), a unit-rate efficiency measure; it is unrelated to SPI (EV/PV), which is the only index that speaks to schedule position.
corrective_rule: Never read a unit-cost/rate index as a schedule statement -- only SPI (built from PV) addresses schedule.
exam_trap: Pairing a correctly-computed index value with a conclusion from a completely different domain (cost-rate vs. schedule) tests whether the candidate tracks what each index actually measures.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Credit$ = 500 x 12 = 6,000; UCI = 6,000/6,500 = 0.92 (correct value, but schedule conclusion is unsupported).

option_identity: UCI = 1.08; quantities exceeded the estimate
option_text: UCI = 1.08; quantities exceeded the estimate
why_wrong: This blends two errors: the 1.08 figure is the same numerator/denominator-reversed reciprocal (Actual$/Credit$) as the first distractor, and the interpretation misattributes the result to quantity growth -- but UCI is specifically constructed (using budget unit cost x ACTUAL quantity) to isolate unit-RATE performance from any quantity effect, so it cannot speak to whether quantities exceeded estimate.
governing_concept: UCI = Credit$/Actual$ (Eq. 19.9) isolates unit-rate performance because Credit$ already uses the actual quantity at the budget rate, cancelling out any quantity variance; UCI says nothing about whether the quantity itself grew.
corrective_rule: UCI's whole purpose is to strip out quantity effects -- never use it to conclude anything about quantity growth.
exam_trap: Combining a reciprocal numeric error with a wrong-domain interpretation (rate vs. quantity) is a compound trap that rewards checking both the number and the concept independently.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Reciprocal = Actual$/Credit$ = 6,500/6,000 = 1.083 (vs. correct UCI = 0.92).
notes: Primary code set to INDEX_RATIO_INVERSION since the numeric error is verified and central; UCI_PI_DOMAIN_CONFUSION also applies to the quantity-attribution error and is noted via secondary_error_class=CONCEPT_GAP.

option_identity: Craft wage rates increased after the budget was established
option_text: Craft wage rates increased after the budget was established
why_wrong: A change in the craft wage rate changes the cost PER UNIT of work, not the number of units installed -- this is a unit-rate variance cause, not a quantity variance cause, even though it still produces a cost overrun overall.
governing_concept: S&K6 attributes cost overruns to two distinct causes: quantities installed exceeding budget quantities (inadequate scope, takeoff errors, scope creep, rework) -- a quantity variance -- versus the actual unit rate (dollars or workhours per unit) exceeding the budget unit rate -- a rate variance (p.264).
corrective_rule: Ask 'did MORE UNITS get installed, or did EACH UNIT cost MORE' -- the former is quantity variance, the latter is rate variance; wage/equipment/overtime rate changes are always rate variance.
exam_trap: The exam offers several plausible, real cost-overrun causes and asks which is specifically a QUANTITY variance -- rate-driven causes (wage, equipment, overtime) are a distinct decomposition category even though they also cause an overrun.

option_identity: Always use Method 3 (historical curves) since it's the most sophisticated
option_text: Always use Method 3 (historical curves) since it's the most sophisticated
why_wrong: The text does not rank Method 3 as universally best or 'most sophisticated'; it explicitly recommends using all three methods together to provide a range of possibilities, never favoring one as the single official method.
governing_concept: 'It is recommended that no single forecasting method be used. Rather, include a forecast by each of the above methods in order to provide a range of possibilities' (p.264).
corrective_rule: Never designate one EAC method as the sole official forecast -- always run and report a range from all applicable methods.
exam_trap: Naming a specific method as 'the best, always use this one' is a direct contradiction of the chapter's explicit no-single-method guidance.

option_identity: Use only whichever method gives the most favorable number for reporting
option_text: Use only whichever method gives the most favorable number for reporting
why_wrong: Selectively reporting only the most favorable EAC is precisely the malpractice the guidance warns against; cherry-picking undermines forecasting's purpose, which is to surface real cost risk, not the best-looking number.
governing_concept: 'It is recommended that no single forecasting method be used... to provide a range of possibilities' (p.264) -- the range exists specifically so management sees the full picture, not a selected favorable outlier.
corrective_rule: Report the range from all methods; never select a single number because it looks better.
exam_trap: This option tests recognition of forecasting integrity, not just formula recall -- a classic 'which practice is unethical/improper' item.

option_identity: Skip EAC forecasting until the project is substantially complete
option_text: Skip EAC forecasting until the project is substantially complete
why_wrong: Delaying EAC forecasting until the project is nearly done defeats its early-warning purpose entirely; forecasting is meant to give management the earliest possible view of cost risk, and waiting eliminates the window for corrective action.
governing_concept: EAC forecasting exists so management has 'a range of possibilities' well before completion, when there is still time to act on unfavorable trends (p.264).
corrective_rule: Produce EAC forecasts throughout the project, not only near completion.
exam_trap: This mirrors a broader project-controls principle (early-warning value of forecasting) that recurs across multiple CCP chapters.

why_wrong: 51,200 = (240/1.20) x 8 x 32, taking the correctly computed total labor-hours needed (200, already representing the whole crew's combined effort) and multiplying by crew size a second time -- double-counting the crew.
governing_concept: Total labor-hours needed = Required Qty / Productivity (240/1.20 = 200 labor-hours, already the crew total); Labor Cost = Labor-Hours x Wage Rate.
corrective_rule: Once total labor-hours already reflects the whole crew's output, never multiply by crew size again.
exam_trap: Double-counting crew size after it has already been absorbed into a productivity-based labor-hour total is a very common estimating slip.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

option_identity: SAR 800
option_text: SAR 800
why_wrong: 800 = days x hours/day x wage (3.125 x 8 x 32), which omits the crew-size factor from the total-cost formula entirely -- it computes cost as if only a single worker, not the full 8-person crew, were being paid.
governing_concept: Labor Cost = Days x Crew Size x Hours/Day x Wage Rate; all four factors are required to get the crew's TOTAL dollar cost.
corrective_rule: Always include crew size as a multiplier in the total labor-cost formula -- dropping it understates cost by a factor of the crew size.
exam_trap: This is the mirror-image error of double-counting crew size: here the crew factor is dropped instead of doubled, producing a far too small a number.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Days x Hours/day x Wage = 3.125 x 8 x 32 = 800 (crew factor of 8 omitted; correct = 800 x 8 = 6,400).
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

why_wrong: 7,360 = 230 x 32, but no single identifiable substitution of the given crew size, hours/day, productivity, wage, or required quantity produces 230 hours through a simple, verifiable calculation step.
governing_concept: Labor Cost = Days x Crew Size x Hours/Day x Wage Rate, computed from crew output/day (76.8 units) and required quantity (240 units).
corrective_rule: Verify every intermediate figure (crew output/day, days required, total labor-hours) against the given inputs rather than accepting a plausible-looking total.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control
notes: Exhaustive 2- and 3-term combinations of the five given inputs (crew, hours/day, productivity, wage, quantity) were checked computationally; none reproduced 230 hours cleanly, so downgraded per rigor rules 2/3.

option_identity: Each new unit requires exactly 80% of the immediately previous unit time.
option_text: Each new unit requires exactly 80% of the immediately previous unit time.
why_wrong: This describes a UNIT learning-curve model (each individual unit takes a fixed percentage of the immediately preceding unit), a different and distinct learning-curve convention from the cumulative-average model the source defines, where the percentage applies to the CUMULATIVE AVERAGE each time cumulative output doubles.
governing_concept: The standard cumulative-average learning curve: average time per unit falls to the learning percentage whenever cumulative quantity doubles -- it is not a flat per-unit-to-previous-unit ratio.
corrective_rule: Confirm which learning-curve convention (cumulative-average vs. unit-curve) a source is using before applying an 80% factor to individual units.
exam_trap: Unit-curve and cumulative-average-curve conventions are both real, legitimate models in the broader literature, making this an easy mix-up even for candidates who understand learning curves generally.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

option_identity: Production capacity must be limited to 80%.
option_text: Production capacity must be limited to 80%.
why_wrong: An 80% learning curve factor describes a rate of improvement in labor time per unit as cumulative output grows -- it has no relationship to capping or limiting production capacity, a completely different operational constraint.
governing_concept: The learning-curve percentage governs how cumulative average labor time per unit declines as cumulative output doubles; it does not constrain how much can be produced.
corrective_rule: A learning-curve percentage describes a LEARNING RATE, never a capacity ceiling.
exam_trap: Unrelated-constraint trap: the learning-curve percentage (a rate of improvement in labor time per unit) is redefined as a cap or limit on production capacity.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

option_identity: Labor cost decreases by 20% every calendar month.
option_text: Labor cost decreases by 20% every calendar month.
why_wrong: The learning curve's percentage reduction is triggered by cumulative OUTPUT doubling, not by the passage of a fixed calendar period; learning curves are a function of cumulative production experience, not elapsed time.
governing_concept: 'Each time cumulative output doubles, the cumulative average labor time per unit becomes 80% of the previous cumulative average' -- the trigger is a doubling of quantity produced, never a calendar interval.
corrective_rule: Learning curves respond to cumulative units produced, not to time elapsed -- a slow month produces less learning than a fast one, all else equal.
exam_trap: Substituting a fixed calendar trigger for the doubling-of-output trigger is a common conceptual shortcut that breaks down whenever production rate varies month to month.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

option_identity: 60 percent
option_text: 60 percent
why_wrong: 60 percent is the credit assigned to the FIRST step -- pipe placed in its permanent location -- not to the end-connections step asked about; the two steps have different, specifically defined percentages.
governing_concept: Example piping rules of credit: pipe placed in permanent location = 60%; end connections welded/bolted = 20%; pipe trim/ready for hydro-test = 20% (p.263).
corrective_rule: Match each rules-of-credit percentage to its own specific step -- do not swap the placement percentage for the connection percentage.
exam_trap: Rules-of-credit questions frequently swap one step's memorized percentage for another's; always re-read which step is being asked about.
source_support: Ch.19, p.263, Measuring Inputs and Outputs

option_identity: 80 percent
option_text: 80 percent
why_wrong: 80 percent is the CUMULATIVE credit after TWO steps are complete (60% placement + 20% end connections), not the marginal 20% credited for completing the end-connections step alone -- this conflates a running cumulative total with the credit for the single step in question.
governing_concept: Example piping rules of credit: pipe placed = 60%; end connections welded/bolted = 20%; trim/hydro-test ready = 20% (p.263) -- each step earns its own listed percentage, not a running total.
corrective_rule: Distinguish the percentage credited FOR a step from the cumulative percentage AFTER that step is reached.
exam_trap: Cumulative-total distractors are a common trap in any step-weighted or rules-of-credit question.
source_support: Ch.19, p.263, Measuring Inputs and Outputs

option_identity: 100 percent
option_text: 100 percent
why_wrong: 100 percent would mean the pipe activity is fully complete (all three steps done: placement, end connections, and trim/hydro-test); completing only the end-connections step earns just its own 20% share, not full credit for the whole activity.
governing_concept: Example piping rules of credit sum to 100% only across all three steps combined: 60% + 20% + 20% = 100% (p.263).
corrective_rule: Full (100%) credit requires ALL listed rules-of-credit steps to be complete, not just the one step named in the question.
exam_trap: Whole-for-part trap: completing one step of a multi-step rules-of-credit activity is credited as if the entire activity (100%) were complete.
source_support: Ch.19, p.263, Measuring Inputs and Outputs

option_identity: The bar chart method, and the CPM method
option_text: The bar chart method, and the CPM method
why_wrong: The bar chart method and CPM (Critical Path Method) are scheduling/network techniques used for time analysis, not labor cost control reporting systems; the source names a completely different pair for cost reporting.
governing_concept: 'The two prevalent construction labor cost control reporting systems are the earned value method and the unit rates method' (p.260, INTRODUCTION).
corrective_rule: Keep scheduling techniques (bar chart, CPM, ADM, PDM) separate from labor cost REPORTING systems (earned value, unit rates) -- they answer different questions.
exam_trap: Substituting well-known scheduling terminology for the specific cost-reporting terminology the chapter defines is an easy trap for candidates who know scheduling but haven't isolated this chapter's specific claim.
source_support: Ch.19, p.260, INTRODUCTION

option_identity: The ADM method, and the PDM method
option_text: The ADM method, and the PDM method
why_wrong: ADM (Arrow Diagramming Method) and PDM (Precedence Diagramming Method) are network scheduling diagramming techniques, not labor cost control reporting systems; the source names a different pair specifically for cost reporting.
governing_concept: 'The two prevalent construction labor cost control reporting systems are the earned value method and the unit rates method' (p.260, INTRODUCTION).
corrective_rule: Keep scheduling network techniques (ADM, PDM) separate from labor cost REPORTING systems (earned value, unit rates).
exam_trap: Wrong-domain-substitution trap: scheduling-diagramming methods (ADM/PDM) are substituted for the source's actual named labor cost control reporting systems (earned value method / unit rates method).
source_support: Ch.19, p.260, INTRODUCTION

option_identity: The Success Index method, and the Productivity Index method
option_text: The Success Index method, and the Productivity Index method
why_wrong: 'Success Index' is not a term defined anywhere in this source; the Productivity Index (PI) IS a real Ch.19 metric, but it is a ratio computed WITHIN the earned value reporting system (Eq. 19.10), not one of the two named overall reporting systems itself.
governing_concept: 'The two prevalent construction labor cost control reporting systems are the earned value method and the unit rates method' (p.260); PI is a sub-calculation inside the earned value method, not a system in its own right.
corrective_rule: Distinguish a system-level reporting method (earned value, unit rates) from a sub-metric computed inside one of those systems (PI, UCI, CPI, SPI).
exam_trap: Mixing a genuine chapter term (Productivity Index) into a fabricated pairing tests whether the candidate can tell a real sub-metric apart from a real overall system.
source_support: Ch.19, p.260, INTRODUCTION

option_identity: Only wage rate, with no other productivity factors recognized
option_text: Only wage rate, with no other productivity factors recognized
why_wrong: Wage rate is not even one of the source's listed productivity factors -- the source explicitly separates the two: 'hourly rates are relatively easy to predict; productivity is the real variable,' and then lists a distinct set of factors (crew size, craft density, interference, scheduling, material/equipment/information availability, rework, site layout, weather, constructability) that affect productivity specifically.
governing_concept: S&K6 lists multiple named factors affecting craft productivity (p.261); wage rate affects labor COST, not productivity, and is explicitly distinguished from it.
corrective_rule: Wage rate and productivity are two separate components of labor cost -- a change in wage rate is never itself a listed 'productivity factor.'
exam_trap: An absolutist 'only X, no other factors' option is nearly always wrong whenever the source provides a multi-item list, as it does here.
source_support: Ch.19, p.261, LABOR COSTS AND PRODUCTIVITY

option_identity: Only the choice of accounting software used for cost coding
option_text: Only the choice of accounting software used for cost coding
why_wrong: Accounting/cost-coding software choice is never named as a factor affecting craft productivity in the source; it belongs to the separate topic of measuring and recording inputs, not to what drives field productivity itself.
governing_concept: S&K6's list of productivity factors (p.261) concerns field/site conditions (crew, density, interference, scheduling, materials, rework, layout, weather, constructability) -- not back-office cost-coding tools.
corrective_rule: Distinguish factors that affect how fast/efficiently craft labor actually performs work from tools used to record and report that work afterward.
exam_trap: Off-list-factor trap: a plausible-sounding but source-unlisted item (e.g., accounting software, contract type alone) is substituted for the source's actual enumerated productivity-factor list.
source_support: Ch.19, p.261, LABOR COSTS AND PRODUCTIVITY

option_identity: Quantity Variance=-32.0 WH (unfavorable), Rate Variance=23.0 WH (favorable)

why_wrong: Both components have their subtraction order reversed: Quantity Variance uses (QF-QB)xPB = (460-500)x0.80 = -32.0 instead of (QB-QF)xPB, and Rate Variance uses QFx(PF-PB) = 460x(0.85-0.80) = +23.0 instead of QFx(PB-PF); the magnitudes match the correct answer but both signs (and thus favorable/unfavorable reads) are flipped.
governing_concept: Quantity Variance = (QB-QF) x PB and Rate Variance = QF x (PB-PF) (Table 19.6); budget quantity/rate must come first in each subtraction for the sign to carry its intended meaning.

corrective_rule: The total net workhour variance is a CHECK on the sum of the two components -- it is never a substitute for computing each component individually.
exam_trap: Mistaking the reconciliation check total for one of the two components it is meant to verify is a specific and instructive trap.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Budget WH (500x0.80=400) - EAC WH (460x0.85=391) = 9.0, reported as Quantity Variance with Rate Variance left at 0 (vs. correct QtyVar=32.0, RateVar=-23.0, which sum to the same 9.0 check total).

governing_concept: Overrun/underrun compares actual cost to EARNED value (percent complete x budget); better/worse performance compares actual unit rate to budget unit rate, where a LOWER actual rate is favorable.
corrective_rule: A lower actual unit rate than budgeted is always BETTER performance, never worse -- fewer resources per unit is efficient.
exam_trap: Correctly identifying the overrun but reversing the efficiency direction is a common 'half right' trap in this two-part question type.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Overrun: 432 vs. earned 400 (50%x800) -> overrun (correct). Unit rate: actual 432/120=3.6 vs. budget 800/200=4.0 -> actual is lower, so performance is better (this option incorrectly says worse).

option_identity: Because inflation always makes future costs lower than present costs
option_text: Because inflation always makes future costs lower than present costs
why_wrong: This both misidentifies the basis for TVM (it is the earning potential/interest on money, not inflation) and gets inflation's typical direction backwards (inflation tends to raise, not lower, future nominal costs).
governing_concept: Time value of money exists because money available now can earn a return over time (the 'rent' for the use of money is interest); it is not grounded in inflation.
corrective_rule: TVM = money can earn a return over time; inflation is a separate, optional adjustment layered on top (constant-dollar/real-rate analysis), not the reason TVM exists.
exam_trap: Attributing the need for discounting to inflation rather than to the earning potential of money (interest).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27, 'Time Value of Money' / Simple vs Compound Interest, Examples 27.1-27.2, p.346

option_identity: Because government regulations require it for capital projects
option_text: Because government regulations require it for capital projects
why_wrong: The source frames TVM as a mathematical/economic necessity (money's earning potential), never as a regulatory mandate.
governing_concept: Time value of money exists because money available now can earn a return over time, so cash flows at different times are not directly comparable without adjustment.
corrective_rule: TVM is a property of money's earning potential, not a compliance requirement imposed by regulation.
exam_trap: Treating an analytical necessity as if it were an external compliance requirement.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27, 'Time Value of Money' / Simple vs Compound Interest, Examples 27.1-27.2, p.346

option_identity: Because it eliminates the need for cash flow forecasting
option_text: Because it eliminates the need for cash flow forecasting
why_wrong: TVM analysis is applied TO forecasted cash flows to make them comparable -- it presupposes forecasting rather than eliminating the need for it.
governing_concept: Engineering economic analysis converts forecasted cash flows at different times to a common, comparable basis using discount factors; it does not remove the forecasting step.
corrective_rule: TVM is a comparison tool applied after cash flows are forecast, not a substitute for forecasting them.
exam_trap: Confusing a tool that processes forecasted cash flows with a tool that removes the need to forecast them.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27, 'Time Value of Money' / Simple vs Compound Interest, Examples 27.1-27.2, p.346

why_wrong: This applies simple (linear) interest growth instead of the compound-growth (F/P) factor the problem requires.
governing_concept: Future value of a present sum under compound growth is F=P(1+i)^n; simple interest instead computes F=P(1+i×n), understating growth for n>1.
corrective_rule: F/P compounds -- (1+i)^n, not (1+i×n). Watch for a wrong option matching the simple-interest total exactly.
exam_trap: Substituting linear (simple-interest) growth for compound growth on a multi-year future-value problem.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27, 'Time Value of Money' / Simple vs Compound Interest, Examples 27.1-27.2, p.346
notes: Exact match to simple-interest growth over 3 years.

why_wrong: This compounds for only 1 year (n=1) instead of the stated 3-year holding period.
governing_concept: F=P(1+i)^n requires n to equal the full stated number of compounding periods (3 years here), not a truncated count.
corrective_rule: Match n to the full stated holding period before compounding -- do not stop at year 1.
exam_trap: Using n=1 (a single compounding period) when the scenario specifies a multi-year holding period.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27, 'Time Value of Money' / Simple vs Compound Interest, Examples 27.1-27.2, p.346
notes: Exact match to F/P with n=1.

why_wrong: This discounts the $600,000 back to a present value (as if it were a known FUTURE amount to be brought to present) instead of compounding it forward, inverting which factor the problem calls for.
governing_concept: Given a present sum invested forward to find its future value, the F/P factor (1+i)^n applies; the reciprocal P/F factor (1+i)^-n brings a future amount back to the present -- the two are not interchangeable.
corrective_rule: F/P carries a present sum FORWARD to a future date; P/F brings a future sum BACK to the present. Match the factor to the direction the cash flow actually moves.
exam_trap: Selecting the inverse engineering-economy factor -- P/F used where F/P was required.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27, 'Time Value of Money' / Simple vs Compound Interest, Examples 27.1-27.2, p.346
notes: Exact match to P/F applied to the present sum, the reciprocal of the correct F/P calculation.

option_identity: Recovering only the interest income earned on an investment
option_text: Recovering only the interest income earned on an investment
why_wrong: Capital recovery restates the FULL investment (principal plus required return) as a uniform annual amount -- it is not limited to the interest/return component alone.
governing_concept: Capital recovery converts a present investment into a uniform annual series that recovers both the principal and the minimum required return over the asset's life, via the (A/P,i,n) 'Uniform Series Capital Recovery' factor.
corrective_rule: Capital recovery = principal recovery + required return, both folded into one uniform annual payment -- not interest alone.
exam_trap: Narrowing capital recovery to only the return/interest portion, dropping the principal-recovery component the (A/P) factor is built to capture.

option_identity: The same calculation as straight-line depreciation
option_text: The same calculation as straight-line depreciation
why_wrong: Straight-line depreciation is a linear accounting allocation of cost (no interest/time value applied); capital recovery uses the compound-interest-based (A/P,i,n) factor and is not the same calculation.
governing_concept: Capital recovery = P(A/P,i,n) [minus S(A/F,i,n) if there is salvage], which embeds the time value of money; straight-line depreciation is simply cost/useful life with no discounting.
corrective_rule: If a capital-recovery amount can be reproduced by dividing cost by years alone, interest has been dropped -- that is depreciation, not capital recovery.
exam_trap: Treating capital recovery (a time-value-of-money calculation) as interchangeable with straight-line depreciation (a non-discounted accounting allocation).

option_identity: The related cash payment clears the bank, regardless of when the obligation arose
option_text: The related cash payment clears the bank, regardless of when the obligation arose
why_wrong: This is the cash-basis recognition rule (recognize only when cash moves), the opposite of accrual accounting, which recognizes the obligation when incurred regardless of payment timing.
governing_concept: Accrual accounting recognizes a cost when the obligation is incurred or the related goods/services are received, not when cash is paid.
corrective_rule: Accrual = recognize when incurred/received; cash basis = recognize only when cash moves. The two bases can recognize the same cost in different periods.
exam_trap: Substituting cash-basis recognition (payment clears the bank) for accrual recognition (obligation incurred).

option_text: The project reaches 100% completion
why_wrong: Accrual recognition happens continuously as obligations are incurred or goods/services are received -- it does not wait for overall project completion.
governing_concept: Cost is recognized under accrual accounting when the obligation is incurred or the related goods/services are received, not tied to a single completion milestone.
corrective_rule: Accrual recognition tracks the incurring event for each obligation, not overall project percent complete.
exam_trap: Tying cost recognition to project completion rather than to the specific event (obligation incurred) that actually triggers it.

why_wrong: Drafting a requisition precedes the obligation being incurred (e.g., a PO issuance or goods/services being received); recognition under accrual accounting attaches to the later, substantive event, not to internal paperwork initiation.
governing_concept: Cost is recognized when the obligation is incurred or goods/services are received -- an earlier internal administrative step (drafting a requisition) does not itself create the obligation.
corrective_rule: Recognition attaches to the event that creates the obligation (commitment/receipt), not to an earlier internal drafting step with no binding effect yet.
exam_trap: Recognizing cost too early, at an internal administrative step that precedes the actual incurring event.

option_identity: Use total projected profit as a substitute for the timing of project cash movements.
option_text: Use total projected profit as a substitute for the timing of project cash movements.
why_wrong: Total projected profit is an aggregate, non-time-phased figure; it cannot reveal WHEN funding or liquidity is needed, which is exactly the near-term expenditure-peak problem described.
governing_concept: Cash flow analysis requires time-phased inflows and outflows to identify funding or liquidity needs -- accounting profit (a period-aggregate, non-cash-timed figure) is not a substitute for that timing information.
corrective_rule: Profit tells you IF a project is worthwhile; time-phased cash flow tells you WHEN money must be available -- the two answer different questions.
exam_trap: Substituting an aggregate profitability figure for the time-phased cash flow analysis a funding/liquidity question actually requires.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Ignore receipt and payment timing because a profitable project will generate sufficient cash over its life.
option_text: Ignore receipt and payment timing because a profitable project will generate sufficient cash over its life.
why_wrong: Lifetime profitability says nothing about whether cash is available during the near-term expenditure peak described -- a profitable project can still face a real liquidity shortfall before receipts catch up.
governing_concept: Time-phased cash flow analysis is needed specifically to identify funding or liquidity needs that overall profitability does not reveal.
corrective_rule: A profitable project over its full life can still run out of cash in the short term -- timing, not lifetime totals, determines liquidity risk.
exam_trap: Assuming eventual profitability eliminates the need to analyze near-term cash timing.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Include capital purchases and omit customer receipts from the cash-flow view.
option_text: Include capital purchases and omit customer receipts from the cash-flow view.
why_wrong: A cash-flow analysis must capture both inflows (receipts) and outflows (expenditures) to identify funding needs -- including only outflows overstates the shortfall and omits the information needed to see when receipts close the gap.
governing_concept: Time-phased cash-flow analysis requires both cash inflows and outflows to correctly identify funding or liquidity needs, not disbursements alone.
corrective_rule: A funding-needs analysis must be symmetric -- both inflows and outflows, time-phased together -- not one side of the ledger only.
exam_trap: Building a cash-flow view that includes outflows but arbitrarily excludes inflows (or vice versa).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Use forecast margin to conclude that external financing is unnecessary.
option_text: Use forecast margin to conclude that external financing is unnecessary.
why_wrong: A positive forecast margin describes eventual profitability, not the near-term cash timing caused by retention and slow certification -- it does not establish that financing is unneeded during the deficit period.
governing_concept: Modeling the timing of collections, retention, and payments is what actually reveals a temporary cash deficit and any required financing period -- margin alone cannot.
corrective_rule: Margin measures eventual profitability; a financing need is a timing question that only a time-phased cash model can answer.
exam_trap: Using an aggregate profitability figure (margin) to dismiss a timing-driven cash/financing question.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Recognize retained revenue as cash received when it is earned for accounting purposes.
option_text: Recognize retained revenue as cash received when it is earned for accounting purposes.
why_wrong: Retained revenue is earned (and may be recognized on an accrual basis for accounting) before it is actually received in cash; treating it as if already received conflates accrual recognition with actual cash-flow timing, masking the very deficit the scenario describes.
governing_concept: Accrual recognition (revenue earned) and cash-flow timing (cash actually received) are distinct; retention specifically withholds cash beyond the point revenue is earned, so a cash-flow analysis must track actual collection timing, not accrual recognition.
corrective_rule: Earned/recognized (accrual) is not the same as received (cash) -- retention is the textbook case where the gap between the two creates a real cash deficit.
exam_trap: Substituting accrual revenue recognition for actual cash receipt timing in a cash-flow/liquidity analysis.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Move subcontractor payments to the client receipt dates without contractual support.
option_text: Move subcontractor payments to the client receipt dates without contractual support.
why_wrong: Cash-flow analysis is meant to identify and model the actual deficit/financing need, not to unilaterally re-time contractual obligations without a supporting contractual basis, which risks breach and does not resolve the underlying timing gap.
governing_concept: The appropriate response is to model the timing of collections, retention, and payments to identify the deficit and required financing period -- not to informally reschedule payment obligations.
corrective_rule: Cash-flow analysis models timing as it actually is (and identifies financing needs); it does not license unilaterally changing payment obligations without contractual basis.
exam_trap: Proposing an unsupported reallocation of payment timing instead of properly modeling and financing the identified deficit.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Exclude repayment deductions because the advance was received before construction started.
option_text: Exclude repayment deductions because the advance was received before construction started.
why_wrong: The repayment deductions are a known, contractually certain future cash outflow; excluding them (for a reason -- timing of the advance -- unrelated to whether they will occur) understates future cash needs.
governing_concept: A time-phased cash-flow forecast must reflect both the advance as an early inflow AND the later repayment deductions as outflows when they occur.
corrective_rule: A known future cash outflow belongs in the forecast regardless of when the related inflow occurred -- timing of receipt does not excuse omitting a known future deduction.
exam_trap: Omitting a known, certain future cash outflow (repayment deductions) from the forecast.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Spread the advance evenly across project months rather than when cash is received and repaid.
option_text: Spread the advance evenly across project months rather than when cash is received and repaid.
why_wrong: A cash-flow forecast must reflect WHEN cash actually moves; spreading the advance evenly across calendar months instead of at its actual receipt/repayment dates misrepresents the real timing of funding availability and need.
governing_concept: The time-phased cash-flow forecast should reflect the advance as an early inflow and the repayment deductions at the actual dates they reduce later invoices, not a flat calendar-uniform allocation.
corrective_rule: Cash flows are time-phased to when cash actually moves, not smoothed evenly across the calendar -- real project cash movement is rarely uniform.
exam_trap: Replacing actual receipt/repayment timing with an artificial uniform monthly spread.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Treat the advance as project profit because it improves early cash position.
option_text: Treat the advance as project profit because it improves early cash position.
why_wrong: A mobilization advance is a liability to be repaid through later invoice deductions, not earned profit; treating it as profit ignores the offsetting repayment obligation and misstates the project's financial position.
governing_concept: The advance should be reflected as an early cash inflow together with its later repayment deductions in the time-phased forecast -- it is a financing/timing mechanism, not earned profit.
corrective_rule: An improved early cash position from an advance is a timing effect, not profit -- the corresponding repayment obligation must also be recognized.
exam_trap: Conflating a temporary, repayable cash inflow (advance) with permanent earned profit.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.27 Financial & Cash Flow Analysis; Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.G

option_identity: Forecast funding from physical percent complete without considering payment timing.
option_text: Forecast funding from physical percent complete without considering payment timing.
why_wrong: Physical percent complete measures work progress, not when cash must actually be disbursed or collected; it does not by itself reveal period-by-period funding requirements or peaks.
governing_concept: Funding requirements are forecast by time-phasing expected expenditures and receipts, not by physical percent complete, which omits payment timing entirely.
corrective_rule: Percent complete answers 'how much work is done'; a funding forecast answers 'when must cash be available' -- time-phased expenditures/receipts, not percent complete, answer the latter.
exam_trap: Substituting physical progress percentage for actual time-phased payment timing when forecasting funding needs.

option_identity: Use cumulative actual cost as the funding forecast and omit future commitments because they are not yet cash outflows.
option_text: Use cumulative actual cost as the funding forecast and omit future commitments because they are not yet cash outflows.
why_wrong: Cumulative actual cost is backward-looking; a funding requirements FORECAST must include expected future expenditures and receipts, not just cost already incurred, or it will understate coming funding needs.
governing_concept: Forecasting funding requirements means time-phasing expected future expenditures and receipts to identify period-by-period needs and funding peaks -- not simply extending cumulative actual cost to date.
corrective_rule: A funding forecast is forward-looking by definition -- cumulative actual cost to date is a historical figure, not a forecast of what is still to come.

why_wrong: BAC is a single, fixed total budget figure -- applying it as the funding requirement for EVERY period would wildly overstate near-term funding needs and provides no period-by-period timing information at all.
governing_concept: Funding requirements are forecast by time-phasing expected expenditures and receipts across periods, not by repeating the total budget (BAC) as if it applied to each period individually.
corrective_rule: BAC is a project-total ceiling, not a per-period figure -- period-by-period funding needs come from time-phasing, not from repeating the total.

option_identity: More than 1.00 percent
option_text: More than 1.00 percent
why_wrong: This reverses the compounding direction: since compounding always pushes the effective annual rate ABOVE 12×the monthly rate, a monthly rate producing exactly a 12.00% effective annual result must be LESS than 1.00%, not more.
governing_concept: If the monthly rate were exactly 1.00% and compounded, the effective annual rate would exceed 12×1.00%=12.00% (because of interest-on-interest); since the stated effective rate is exactly 12.00%, the underlying monthly rate must be below 1.00%.
corrective_rule: Compounding always makes the effective annual rate exceed (periodic rate × periods per year); to hit a GIVEN effective rate exactly, the periodic rate must be somewhat BELOW that simple division.
exam_trap: Reversing the direction of the compounding effect -- assuming the periodic rate must be higher, when compounding means it must be lower, to reach a stated effective annual rate.
source_support: CCP Certification Study Guide, 2nd Ed. -- Chapter 27, 'Effective interest rate' topic, Check on Learning Q1/Solution, pp.180-189

option_identity: 1.00 percent
option_text: 1.00 percent
why_wrong: This assumes the monthly rate needed is simply 12.00%/12=1.00%, i.e. that compounding has no effect -- but if 1.00%/month WERE compounded, the resulting effective annual rate would exceed 12.00%.
governing_concept: 1.00% per month compounded for 12 months would yield an effective annual rate greater than the simple 12×1.00%=12.00%, because each month's interest also earns interest; to land exactly at a 12.00% effective rate, the monthly rate must be under 1.00%.
corrective_rule: Simple division (effective/periods) gives the rate that would apply WITHOUT compounding; with compounding, the true periodic rate needed is always somewhat lower.
exam_trap: Treating the linear (effective rate ÷ periods) division as if it already accounted for compounding.
